grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('Waswera')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'Waswera'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('tinogona')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'tinogona' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

cultural_notes.title: Phone Etiquette in Shona: Always Starting with 'Waswera Sei?'
cultural_notes.content: Even when making a quick phone call to arrange a meeting ('kusangana nhasi'), a Shona speaker never jumps straight to the request—they always open warmly with 'Waswera sei?' ('How have you spent the day?').

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new morning exchange into English: 'Mangwanani baba, mamuka sei?'
options: Good evening Mother, how was your day?
Hello my friend, where are you going today?
Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.correct_answer: Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mangwanani' = 'Good morning', 'baba' = 'Father', and 'mamuka sei?' = 'how did you wake up?'.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'two women and four men' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vakadzi vaviri' = 'two women' (-viri = 2) and 'nevarume vana' = 'and four men' (-na = 4).
